policy_title: Abolish Business Rates for high street SMEs and introduce Online Delivery Tax
stated: Reform UK will abolish Business Rates for high street-based Small and Medium Sized Enterprises (SMEs), offsetting this with a 4% Online Delivery Tax for large, multinational enterprises to create a fairer playing field. They will also cut entrepreneurs' tax to 5%.

source.quote: Abolish Business Rates for high street based SMEs. Offset this with Online Delivery Tax at 4% for large, multinational enterprises to create a fairer playing field for high streets. Cut entrepreneurs’ tax to 5%.

bearing_set.reason: Abolishing business rates for high street SMEs directly alters the cost-base and viability of small employers, affecting jobs, business formation and working conditions in that sector; the entrepreneurs' tax cut to 5% further shapes incentives to start and scale businesses.

A 4% Online Delivery Tax on large multinationals would plausibly be passed on (in whole or part) to consumers through higher delivery charges or retail prices, materially affecting household costs for online shoppers.
Abolishing business rates for high-street SMEs and cutting entrepreneurs' tax to 5% directly affects business formation, SME survival, and aggregate economic dynamism and living standards.
Entrepreneurs' tax cut to 5% and business rates abolition are direct reductions in the tax burden on SME owners and entrepreneurs, materially changing take-home returns.

Business rates raise ~£26bn/year in England; even partial abolition for SMEs is a large revenue loss whose offset via a new online delivery tax is unverified — if the offset falls short, the funded/borrowed balance worsens materially.

Entrepreneurs' tax cut primarily benefits business owners (typically higher-income); the online delivery tax, if passed to consumers, falls disproportionately on lower-income households who increasingly shop online — a real distributional shift in the rich-poor gap.

membership_note: Five fundamentals cleared the non-negligible bar: the core economic effect (O13), direct tax-burden changes for entrepreneurs and SME owners (O11), a concrete consumer-price mechanism from the delivery tax (O2), an uncertain fiscal offset risk (O12), and a distributional asymmetry between beneficiaries and likely payers of the delivery tax (O14).
